mcqs.question: Why should a pipeline's test stage consume the build stage's output artifact rather than re-checking-out and recompiling the source itself?
options: Otherwise build and test can silently compile different bits, so a passing test says nothing about the artifact that will actually ship
Recompiling in the test stage is slower but produces an identical, equally valid artifact
Test stages are only allowed to run static analysis, never a real build
It reduces the number of stages the pipeline needs to define
mcqs.explanation: If test recompiles instead of consuming build's artifact directly, a nondeterministic build step or a dependency resolving differently a moment later means the tests validated something other than what will actually be packaged and shipped. Speed isn't the core issue — correctness of the handoff is, and stage count is unrelated.

mcqs.question: A team rebuilds their service from source separately for staging and production instead of promoting one artifact. What does this put at risk?
options: Nothing, as long as both builds use the same source commit
The staging pass becomes meaningless as a signal, because production may resolve dependencies or bake config differently and run a subtly different binary
Only the build's compile time is affected, not correctness
It only matters for compiled languages, not interpreted ones
mcqs.explanation: Same source commit doesn't guarantee same binary — a floating dependency version, a build-time environment variable, or a timing difference can produce a different artifact even from identical source. That breaks the entire point of a staging gate. The risk is a correctness one, not merely a speed cost, and it applies to interpreted languages too if their dependency resolution isn't pinned.

mcqs.question: A pipeline's dependency cache is keyed on branch name instead of a lockfile hash. What's the risk?
options: A branch can restore a stale cached dependency set even after the lockfile changed, silently testing outdated dependencies
The cache will simply never hit, making the pipeline slower but not incorrect
Branch-based cache keys are actually the recommended pattern for dependency caching
It only affects container layer caching, not dependency caching
mcqs.explanation: A cache key should change exactly when the thing it caches changes — that's the lockfile hash, not the branch name. Keying on branch means a lockfile bump on that branch can still restore the old, stale dependency set, which is a correctness bug wearing a performance-optimization disguise, not just a missed speedup.

mcqs.question: When is a build matrix (testing across multiple OS/language-version combinations) worth its extra CI cost?
options: Always, since more coverage is unconditionally better regardless of the project
For a library or SDK supporting a wide range of runtimes its users actually run, where an untested combination is a real, likely-to-be-hit gap
Only for projects with fewer than 100 commits
Never — a matrix is purely a legacy pattern superseded by containerization
mcqs.explanation: A matrix trades CI cost for coverage, so it pays off exactly where the support surface is genuinely wide and untested combinations are plausible in the wild — a public library, not a service that only ever runs one OS/runtime combo in production. "Always" ignores the cost side, and matrices remain relevant even for containerized workloads that still vary by language runtime.

mcqs.question: Staging passes, but production — rebuilt separately hours later — breaks on a code path staging never exercised. What's the actual defect?
options: The application code has a hidden bug that only staging happened to avoid
The pipeline design treated two separately-built artifacts as one validated artifact, so the staging pass gave no real guarantee about what production actually ran
The test suite didn't have enough coverage of that code path
Production servers have different hardware than staging
mcqs.explanation: The root cause is architectural: rebuilding per environment lets a transitive dependency resolve differently between the two builds, so "staging passed" was never actually a statement about the bytes running in production. More test coverage wouldn't have caught this, because the two environments ran genuinely different artifacts — the fix is build-once-promote, not more tests.
